issues.description: The stated reason for dismissing Lake Herman Road ('exists only in the modern WGS84 / NOAA solver frame') is partly wrong. The 1-rad-ccw bearing does not depend on the datum. Anyone with an accurate 1970 map (USGS quad, about 17 deg E printed) and a compass on the summit gets it (decl 17.0 gives 1.0018 rad). What fails on the mailed sheet is narrower: its printed N arrow is 4.6 deg west of true north (giving 0.92 rad), and a paper inch covers 7.0 ground miles (2.75 in, not 3). The '3 in' needs an accurate ground distance converted at the label scale of 6.4. The conclusion is unchanged, but this reason is overstated.

The face-value p-values for the Lake Herman Road coincidence come from post-hoc narrow families, and one range end is misquoted. The report's upper bound '0.089 (9 sites)' is the S9 'pairs + bearings, 6 refs' row. The S9 'everything, 6 refs' row is 0.146 (N1) / 0.158 (N2). My wider grid-hit family adds true N, magnetic E and true E zeros (Foxon's polar axis) and a rotation null that preserves the real site constellation. For integer k and n it gives p(<=obs) 0.010-0.016, p(<=0.25 mi) 0.034-0.053 and p(<=0.5 mi) 0.12-0.18. Adding half-inch n and the 7.0 scale gives 0.04-0.06 / 0.12-0.18 / 0.35-0.50.

The 0.019 deg error is false precision. 0.1 mi of uncertainty in the LHR site position moves the bearing 0.30 deg. Declination 16.5 to 17.0 moves it -0.40 to +0.10 deg. The LHR coordinate is Wikipedia's location-map value; the attacker did not source the actual turnout (pumping-station gate) independently, although the task said 're-derive'. Only the tolerance-based p-values mean anything.

The drawn 0-arm angle is over-precise. The reported 3.02 deg with bootstrap sd 0.07 only reflects pixel noise. My independent ink fits give 1.9-3.2 deg depending on mask threshold and segments: the inner circle segments fit about 2.0 deg, the outer about 3.1. The arm is a freehand curve. A realistic statement is 2.5 +- 0.6 deg (true bearing -1.4 to -2.6 deg). The conclusion that the 0 does not point to magnetic north is unaffected.

Penn's watch face is framed loosely ('7:04 is a free parameter'). The circle through Berryessa (12:00) and the summit has one free parameter. Forcing Blue Rock Springs exactly onto 9:00 puts the summit at 7:00, 60.1 deg from the 9:00 radius: 2.81 deg (4.9%) more than one radian. That is the same miss as the direct summit angle of 60.28 deg. Penn's 58 deg is not reproduced. This strengthens the negative verdict.

Foxon's (12 in, 3 rad) and (3 in, 0 rad) were tested with zero = magnetic north, not his stated polar axis (east, counter-clockwise). I re-tested in his convention: polar axis true E, magnetic E or map-right, at scale 6.4 or 7.01, 12 variants. All fall off the mailed inset: 12 in is 77-84 mi out; 3 in east is 19-21 mi against an east reach of 1.13-1.16 in. The conclusion stands.

The school test uses a null that is not spatially matched to the grid. Land grid points have a median distance of 14.0 mi from the summit, against 23.8 mi for the 96 random null points. Grid points cluster in rural park land, which pushes the grid's school rate down relative to the null. Within distance strata the comparison flips: beyond 15 mi, 11.9% (grid, n=109) vs 8.5% (null, n=71) at 0.25 mi. Under 15 mi, 2.9% vs 8.0% (null n=25). Further problems: the baseline rests on 8 hits; only 37 of 92 points in the solver-frame grid were annotated; the data are 2026 OSM. The school result is uninformative rather than negative evidence. A matched null (randomly rotated grids) was not run.

A coincidence listed in research/z32_map.md was not evaluated. The July 26 doodle's bold zero sits at 241-242 deg, against the Stine site's 1970 magnetic bearing of 241.03 deg (0.47 deg off). Analytic look-elsewhere at +-1 deg over 13 sites and 1-2 references gives p = 0.07-0.14, so it is not significant. It should still have been reported.

report.conclusion:
Neither cipher carries enough information to pick out a plaintext, and we found no reading of either that beats the null.

**Computed: Z13.** About 1 in 2.1 million real English 13-letter windows fits Z13 with homophones allowed (21.0 bits of constraint); about 1 in 9.3 million fits as a simple substitution (23.2 bits). That is 5.6 times more often than uniformly random letters, which is where Oranchak's '1 in 12 million' comes from (26^5).
- How many English strings fit depends entirely on how predictable the plaintext is: about 8,000 under our 6-gram model (1,100 if word-aligned), about 190 at 2.2 bits/letter, and below 1 only if the plaintext were as redundant as long running text.
- An isolated phrase or a name does not have long-text redundancy. Under a generic English prior the best reading we know (IN THE DESERT IS) has about 1% posterior.
- Within a FIRST LAST name model the 'best' name has about 45%, but the winner flips between homophonic and strict mode, and the prior that Z13 is such a name at all is unknown.
- Z13's repeat profile is about 2,600 times more likely under a simple-like key than under a Zodiac-style 63-symbol cycling key: 0 of 100,000 English windows reproduce it under cycling.
- Our solver recovers simple-key ciphers of Z13's length about 3% of the time.

**Computed: Z32.**
- About 1 in 3,800 English 32-letter windows fits, only 11.9 bits of constraint against at least 73 bits of window entropy.
- That leaves about 10^17 to 10^19 fitting strings under the 6-gram model, and still about 10^6 under the most generous 1.0 bit/letter assumption.
- Simple substitution is impossible because Z32 has 29 symbols and English has 26 letters.
- Every published Z32 reading has a posterior of 10^-20 or less under a generic prior.
- Our homophonic solver needs 200-340 letters before it recovers a 63-symbol key, and recovered 0 of 12 at 32 letters.

**Computed: solver null.**
- The solver sees only the isomorph, so it returns the same English for every plaintext that fits; it beat the true plaintext's score in 20/20 (Z13) and 12/12 (Z32) synthetic cases.
- The real ciphers' best scores are typical of random isomorphs with the same repeat profile.

**Computed: Oranchak 2013 reproduced.**
- Names: our FIRST LAST homophonic hit rate of 1 in 2.08 million matches his 1 in 2 million. His 213 fits are simply his number of tests times that rate.
- Words: his 283 two-word and 1,283,443 three-word fits are reproduced to the right order of magnitude. Ours range from 113 to 4,772 two-word and 363k to 114M three-word fits, depending only on the word list. His fits were homophonic, not strict, judging from his examples.

**What this means for claims.** Any claimed Z13 or Z32 solution has to bring information from outside the cipher: a key carried over from another cipher, a method that predicts something checkable, or a validated link to the map. Fitting the symbols and reading as English is expected by chance.

**Assumed.**
- The corpus is 1850-1945 American fiction.
- Entropy figures are cross-entropy upper bounds from our 6-gram model.
- The posteriors assume the plaintext is a random English window and that the key adds no information.

**Speculation.** The relative likelihood of the key models depends on the cycling and allocation rules in encrypt.js.

The data/ciphers/README.md does not contradict the task's foundation facts. Isomorphic variants give identical counts, as the README implies.
caveats: Z13 counts are small (53 homophonic and 12 strict windows), so the constraint bits have 95% CIs of about +/-0.4 bits (homophonic) and +/-0.9 bits (strict).

Windows with three identical letters in a row are excluded as junk ('clean'). For Z13 every excluded window was junk, such as EEEEEEEEEEEEE. For Z32 the filter also drops up to 203 legitimate windows (0.7%), such as SUCCESS SHE, which shifts C by under 0.01 bits.

Expected solution counts span orders of magnitude depending on the assumed entropy per letter. Meaning is not captured by any model we have. The 6-gram figures are upper bounds; the 1.0-1.3 bits/letter figures assume long-text redundancy, which a 13-letter name or isolated phrase lacks.

The 6-gram model is about 0.43 bits (13 letters) and 1.75 bits (32 letters) more confident on training windows than on held-out ones. The Z13 conditional-entropy estimate uses training windows because the held-out set has only one fit.

Solver null: synthetic ciphers with the exact isomorph pose the same problem as the real cipher. Their truths are arbitrary corpus windows, mostly not word-aligned, which the solver's word term penalises; that widens the truth-vs-best score gap. Only 11 strict Z13 windows exist, so the simple-mode exact set has n = 11, and the Z32 exact and scrambled sets have n = 12 each (time).

The planned dictionary-fit comparison for scrambled Z13 isomorphs (tools/nullmodel_scrambled_enum.js) never ran: it waited 120 minutes for a machine slot and gave up. No results/nullmodel/scrambled_enum.json exists.

Length scan settings: 54 restarts for L <= 64; 24 for L >= 75, except 2 of the 10 zodiac63 L=75 rows, which used 36. 12 ciphers per point at L 13-50, 10 above. encrypt.js gives homophones only to letters present in each plaintext, and the length scan used that default; the key-likelihood test gave every letter at least one symbol.
Key-model likelihoods for exact isomorphs are mostly zero-hit upper bounds; only the repeat-profile likelihoods are firm numbers.

Oranchak's 150k-word dictionary and his 100-million real-name database are not available. Our name lists combine every first name with every surname (24,490 x 175,879), so we compare per-combination rates rather than raw counts.

Two exploratory runs of the tuple counter ran out of memory at their 6 GB heap limit: a 4-word count on the 60k list, and the 3-word Norvig counts under an earlier breadth-first version. I could not stop the 4-word run (process stop was refused); it ended on its own at the limit. All reported tuple counts come from the later depth-first counter (tools/nullmodel_tuplejoin.js). It agrees exactly with tools/enumerate.js on a 5,000-word list and with the earlier trie counter. Where distinct-string counts were capped at 3,000,000, the tuple counts are still exact.

To use a machine slot I already held, I appended the solver-null and length-scan steps to a script that was running in that slot (tools/nullmodel_oranchak_tuples.sh). Each step is bounded by restart counts or --max-seconds. Two queued duplicates (solver null and length scan A) were made harmless with lock and 'already complete' guards.
Not verified here: the Z408 and Z340 plaintexts were never handled; the task did not require them.

- "1 in 12,000,000" is 26^8/26^13. That is the weak (homophonic) uniform figure, so the attacker is right and research/z13_literature.md line 128 and keys_methods.md mislabel it as strict.
- Names: about 0.5e9 tests, 213 fits, "about 1 hit for every 2,000,000 attempts". This matches our FIRST LAST homophonic rate of 4.8e-7.

issues.description:
The solver null and the length scan measure the anneal objective, not English probability. That objective is the sum of joint 5-gram window scores plus a word term (weight 1) and an entropy penalty, and it is not a likelihood. With --score markov --n 6 (log10 P6, the project's own 6-gram model) the same annealer gives these results:
- Z13 simple: returns IN THE DESERT IS (log10 P6 -8.36) in 8 of 54 restarts. The attacker's answer, AN THE WERE STAR, is about 8,500 times less probable (-12.29).
- Exact-isomorph simple set: Markov recovers 1/11 (the DESERT truth); the attacker reported 0/11. Under P6, 10 of 11 truths outrank the attacker's solver output. In the homophonic set, 5 of 20 truths outrank IN THE RESENT IS; for Z32, 4 of 12.
- Length scan, simple keys: L13 4/12 recovered (the attacker had 1/12), L20 1/12 (0/12), L32 9/12 (8/12).
- At L20 three and at L32 two of the Markov failures are search failures: the truth has a higher P6 than the returned string.

So 'best beats truth 20/20, 11/11, 12/12' and 'it always returns different English that scores higher than the truth' describe this objective only. 'Recovers Z13-length simple ciphers about 3% of the time' becomes about 33% (4/12, Wilson 95% CI 14-61%) with a MAP objective.

The headline 'Neither cipher carries enough information to pick out a plaintext' is overstated for Z13 under a strict-substitution, fluent-phrase hypothesis.
- The typical-set count 2^(H-C) (hundreds to thousands of fits) does not govern recovery. The posterior mass of the most probable fit does, and the MAP experiment shows that is the truth for about one third of 13-letter sentence-start phrases.
- The DESERT posterior of 1e-2 uses the homophonic denominator and an arbitrary-window prior. In strict mode the figure is 4e-2 (P6/f_strict).
- Under a word-aligned strict prior it is plausibly of order 0.1-0.5 (crude: only 1 word-aligned strict fit in 6.1M aligned corpus windows).

The right inference is different: under that hypothesis Z13's MAP reading is IN THE DESERT IS, which is nonsense after 'My name is'. That is evidence against 'Z13 = simple-substitution ordinary English phrase', not proof that Z13 is information-starved. The attacker's conclusion does hold under the homophonic hypothesis and under the name hypothesis.

The zodiac63 length-scan points at short lengths are degenerate by construction.
- Following encrypt.js's default, the scan gives homophones only to letters present in each plaintext, so all 63 symbols land on about 9-15 letters.
- As a result, the synthetic L13 and L20 ciphers had 13/13 and 20/20 distinct symbols, and 9 of the 12 L32 ciphers had no repeated symbol at all. Such a cipher has zero constraint, any string fits, and 0% recovery is guaranteed whatever the solver. The solver returned the same string (ANDTHETHEREIS, AGAINSTANDTHETHEREAL) for all 12 at L13 and L20.
- Placing Z32 'like the 63-symbol L32 point with 31.7 distinct symbols' is therefore misleading: Z32 has 3 repeats and 11.9 bits of constraint.

The valid comparison is the exact-isomorph solver null (0/12). The 200-340-letter estimate for homophonic unicity is unaffected, because by then nearly all letters are present.

The 'posteriors' P6(W)/f are not normalized.
- The 6-gram model gives EEEEEEEEEEEEE log10 P6 = -6.35, which is 0.95 of the clean homophonic fit fraction f by itself.
- The junk strings in the corpus fit list sum to 1.87 f, while the 47 clean observed fits sum to only 0.024 f.
- Under the literal 6-gram prior, the homophonic MAP of Z13 is EEEEEEEEEEEEE. Excluding junk, it is THERE WE WERE TW (-8.14), which is above DESERT (-8.36).

The reported posteriors (1e-2, 1.2e-4, 1e-20.6, ...) are relative indices, not probabilities. No conclusion rests on their absolute values.

The word-aligned expected-solution counts pair the word-aligned window entropy with the any-window constraint bits C. With the word-aligned C (20.54 bits homophonic, 22.54 strict):
- Z13 homophonic: 1.5e3 (95% range 4.2e2-4.0e3), not 1.1e3.
- Z13 simple: 386 (range 10-2.2e3), not 253.
- Z32: 2.6e18, not 3.2e18.

The Z13 word-aligned figures rest on 4 and 1 corpus windows, so they are uncertain by an order of magnitude.

Calling Oranchak's word counts 'reproduced to the right order of magnitude' is generous.
- The Norvig 147k and 322k lists contain all 676 two-letter strings and 9,639 / 12,951 three-letter strings. That is token junk, not a dictionary, and it inflates the counts: 857 / 18.2M and 4,772 / 114M.
- Only the Gutenberg list (421 / 1.72M) comes within about 1.5x of his 283 / 1,283,443. The cleanest list (common 59k) gives 113 / 363k.

Accurate wording: his numbers are bracketed by list-dependent counts; the rate per candidate tuple (about 3-4e-7) is what agrees. His homophonic mode is now confirmed by the source.

The Z32 posteriors of the published radians readings (1e-20 to 1e-25) under a fiction 6-gram prior mostly measure how rare RADIANS is in fiction, so they say little about the readings. A topic-matched null shows the readings are unremarkable:
- 20,181 of 47,730,756 grammar-built 32-letter radian/inch phrases fit Z32 (1 in 2,365).
- The fitting phrases include ESTIMATE FOUR RADIANS AND FIVE INCHES and trivial siblings such as ESTIMATE NINE RADIANS DIG FIVE INCHES and ESTIMATE ZERO RADIANS GO THREE INCHES.

This strengthens the negative Z32 conclusion with a fairer yardstick.

The exact-isomorph solver null is not 20 (or 11, 12) independent trials. The solver sees only the isomorph, so every run returns the same answer: one solver output compared against n truths. Its recovery rate is just the corpus frequency of truths equal to that one output. For the Markov MAP in strict mode that is 2 of 12 strict windows (IN THE DESERT IS occurs twice), not 0.

The FIRST LAST name posterior uses a first-name prior that ignores sex. Most of the top names are female (CHASTITY, ELSIE, IMOGENE, IRENE, ADRIANA), and the 'best' name flips with the mode. The attacker already labels it not evidence, but conditioning on male names is the obvious missing refinement.

In the key-model comparison, '>2,600:1 against 63-symbol cycling' rests on 0/100,000 hits under perfectly strict cycling. Zodiac's real cycling was about 90%, and the random-selection model already gives 6.6e-4, so a realistic mixed model would cut the ratio to roughly 100:1. The attacker flags this as speculation.

candidate_verdicts.reason: It fits Z13 strictly and is the MAP reading under the 6-gram Markov objective in strict mode (log10 P6 -8.36, 8 of 54 restarts). Its posterior is 4e-2 under an arbitrary-window strict prior and of order 1e-1 under a word-aligned prior (one window, poorly determined). It is nonsense after 'My name is', and it was itself a corpus window. It does not beat the null; at most it marks what a strict-phrase hypothesis predicts.

It is an artifact of the joint-5-gram objective: the solver returns it for every plaintext with this isomorph. It is 76 times less probable under the 6-gram model than IN THE DESERT IS, and a Markov 6-gram solve does not return it.

Homophonic fit only (two symbols for D and two for E). Its 0.43 posterior holds only under a sex-agnostic, population-weighted FIRST LAST prior with a constant likelihood across weak fits, and the top name flips to CHASTITY TRACY in strict mode. No evidence beyond the null.

It starts with a fragment and is the same kind of word salad the solver returns for random scrambled isomorphs (8 of 12 scored at least as high). Under P6, 4 of 12 random fitting truths outrank solver outputs like it.

It fits homophonically, but Z32 imposes only 11.9 bits. One in 2,365 phrases from a small radian/inch grammar fits (20,181 fits, including ESTIMATE NINE RADIANS DIG FIVE INCHES). It was built using the July 26 hint, so fitting is expected by construction.

review.adjusted_conclusion:
**Z32: the attacker's result stands and is robust.**
- About 1 in 3,800 English windows fit Z32 (11.89 bits, reproduced exactly).
- Simple substitution is impossible.
- On a topic-matched null, 1 in 2,365 grammatical radian/inch phrases fits as well, so no published or solver reading beats the null.

**Z13 counts: reproduced exactly.**
- 53 / 112,021,522 homophonic windows (21.0 bits); 12 strict (23.2 bits).
- Oranchak's figures are explained: 1 in 12M = 26^5 (weak, uniform), 1 in 670k = the iid figure, and 1 in 2M names = our 4.8e-7.

**Z13 solver-based statements are objective-dependent and must be revised.** The anneal objective (joint 5-gram plus word term) is not the language-model likelihood. A MAP solver using the 6-gram Markov score:
- recovers 4 of 12 13-letter simple-key phrases, not 1 of 12;
- returns IN THE DESERT IS for Z13 in strict mode;
- ranks 10 of the 11 strict corpus truths above the attacker's answer.

Under a strict-substitution, fluent-phrase hypothesis, Z13 is therefore at the edge of solvability, not far below it. Its MAP reading is nonsensical after 'My name is', which counts against that hypothesis. Under the homophonic hypothesis or a name hypothesis, the attacker's 'no unique solution' conclusion holds.

**Other corrections.**
- The zodiac63 length-scan points at L13, L20 and L32 had no repeated symbols, so they say nothing; the exact-isomorph solver null is the valid Z32 comparison.
- The 6-gram 'posteriors' are unnormalized: EEEEEEEEEEEEE alone gets 0.95 f.

No candidate is supported.

report.conclusion:
Computed: Z13 does not single out any English phrase. On canonical Z13 (AENz0K0M0[NAM), an exhaustive search over the whole 60,006-word common list with up to 5 words finds 25.8M strings consistent with simple substitution and 148.8M consistent with homophonic substitution. That word space contains 100% of real held-out 13-letter phrases that score above the median. Of those strings, only 22 (simple) and 64 (homophonic) reach the median real-phrase score of -9.861. 1 and 3 reach p75, and none reaches p90. The other variants give similar or larger counts: reversed 11/54, crosshair-as-null 1/5 at the 12-letter median, letters-literal 0/0. The circles-distinct variant has hundreds of good fits (incomplete runs) plus 3 one-word fits. No single word in the 333k vocabulary fits any variant except circles-distinct.

The good fits are mostly word salad. 3 of the 22 simple fits and 9 of the 64 homophonic fits pass a corpus-trigram grammaticality proxy, versus 84% of real phrases. The ones that pass are fragments (ON THE DEFEAT OF, IN THE DESERT IS), not a name or a message. No Zodiac-themed word appears among the main canonical runs' above-median fits.

Allowing null letters at the ends, or one miswritten symbol, adds more generic fits (OTHER EVENTS, OF THE DIRECTOR) and no meaningful ones. Published readings are reproduced (ACHIEVE LETHAL ranks 23rd and SARAH THE HORSE 43rd) but none is distinguished.

Assumed: the LM (Norvig Web 1T words plus fiction-trained letter n-grams) is a fair English prior, and the median of real held-out phrases is a fair bar for "good English".

Calibration: 20,000 real phrases encrypted with Zodiac-style homophonic keys (54 or 63 symbols, cycled) never give 8 or fewer distinct symbols, or a triple inside 5 positions. Simple substitution does so 24% and 10% of the time. So if Z13 is English, it is closer to simple substitution than to the Z408/Z340 systems.

Speculation: none of the candidates should be put forward. The headline bound is that a 13-symbol cipher with this pattern admits roughly 20 to 60 equally good English readings under the stated vocabulary, and hundreds if the circles differ or a slip or nulls are allowed. Z13 alone cannot confirm any reading as a phrase.
caveats: Not completed because of shared-slot contention: the waits were 53 and 67 minutes. As a result: circles_distinct at 60k/<=5 in both modes (killed; the first task did not finish in 6 and 24 minutes); the full-vocabulary 3-word runs (only canonical simple was attempted, a 12-task sample of which 6 tasks finished, so it is not exhaustive); homophonic slips; homophonic null-end runs; the 6-word runs (coverage already shows 6 words add nothing above the median); and the truth-rank calibration (tools/z13phrases_calib.js enum was written but never run).

Slip runs used the top 20,000 words and up to 4 words, not 60k/5 (covers 93.7% of above-median real phrases). Their baseline is the 60k/5 canonical simple run restricted to that space. The pooled slip posterior uses a heuristic prior.

Homophonic posterior shares cover only scored fits (bound at or above the real p25). The bound histogram gives only a loose bound on the unscored mass for those runs. Simple-mode posteriors are accurate (unscored mass estimated below 3e-5 of the scored mass).

The grammaticality proxy is crude. It checks that every word trigram (or the bigram for two words) occurs within a sentence of the training corpus, and it lets some nonsense through. That check covered only runs written before 15:54 UTC (main runs, full1, full2). Null-end and slip runs are categorised with the weaker Web 1T bigram-chain proxy (attestationChecked=false in summary.json).

The word LM is modern web text (Norvig Web 1T), so it favours modern tokens (DATABASE, EMAIL, BENETTON). The full 333k vocabulary contains web junk tokens such as OFTHESE, and the scores do not reflect 1970 usage.

The categories (name-like, theme) are list-based. name_tokens.tsv excludes the 5,000 most common words. theme_words.txt is a curated list of 93 words. plaintext_vocab.txt is derived from the Z408/Z340 plaintexts and was never printed.

Queued jobs were changed through results/z13phrases/overrides.json: the slip runs went to 20k/<=4, and full3_canonical was sampled and capped. Each output records this in options.overrides. Some low-priority jobs were skipped by writing claim files (since removed).

TSV streams hold only fits at or above each run's stream threshold (simple: real p10; homophonic: p25; slips and ends: p25 or p50; handles: all). Counts at thresholds at or above tlow are exact. full2_circles_distinct_simple.tsv was truncated by a killed rerun, but its JSON top list is intact.
z13.bracket_is_perp has the same pattern as the canonical string, so it gives identical results without key pins. It was not run separately.
Self-test (logs/selftest.log): the driver matches tools/enumerate.js fit for fit, the score bound held on 8,006 strings, and the posterior, slip and range options were checked.

review.reproduction_notes:
I reran four load-bearing computations, each through tools/run_slot.js with 4 threads. Every compared field came out identical. Script: results/z13phrases/review/run_review.sh; comparison logs: results/z13phrases/review/compare_*.log.
(1) Real-phrase null (node tools/z13phrases_null.js --n 4000): identical percentiles. 13 letters: median -9.8613, p75 -8.3388, p90 -7.1913, p99 -6.0071.
(2) w60k5 canonical simple: 25,761,330 consistent strings; 22 at or above the median, 1 at or above p75, 0 at or above p90. topShare 0.2156, effN 43.25. All 2,178 streamed top fits are identical.
(3) w60k5 canonical homophonic: 148,816,201 strings; 64 / 3 / 0; the 1,081-fit top list is identical.
(4) slip06 simple 20k/4: 14,642,015 strings; 239 at or above the median; best OF THE DIRECTOR -5.8281; the first 2,000 fits are identical.
Independent checks I wrote:
- tools/z13phrases_review_brute.js is a naive word-by-word counter with no trie and no state machine. It matches the driver at five settings: simple 5k/3 = 208; homophonic 3k/3 = 348; simple 5k/3 with a slip at 6 = 6,662; simple 2k/4 = 1,458; simple 5k/3 with range 1:12 = 30,676 (results/z13phrases/review/brute.log).
- tools/z13phrases_review_oneword.js scans all 333k words. There are 0 one-word fits for canonical, reversed, crosshair_null and letters_literal in both modes. circles_distinct homophonic has 3: SLEEPLESSNESS, STEADFASTNESS, TROUBLESHOOTS.
- The variant strings are right: reversed is the exact reverse; crosshair_null drops position 3; the letters_literal pins are recorded in options.pin.
- boundViolations is 0 in every run. The top 500 fits of the main runs are all consistent with their cipher and mode. The slip fits are consistent once the wildcard position is removed.
The code audit found no bias-producing bug in the enumeration, the scoring bound, the variant handling or the threshold logic. The problems are in calibration and interpretation (below).

issues.description: The headline counts were never compared with a null, and the attacker never ran its own calibration (tools/z13phrases_calib.js enum). I ran it at reduced scale (tools/z13phrases_review_calib.js; simple substitution, 20k words, at most 4 words; results/z13phrases/review/calib_profile.json). Z13 is typical of both 25 random rearrangements of its own 13 symbols (same 3,2,2,2,1,1,1,1 profile) and 25 real held-out phrases with that profile. Fits at or above the median: Z13 22; scrambles median 13 (range 0-33), 20% at 22 or more; English median 12 (range 1-92), 28% at 22 or more. Best fit: Z13 -8.31; scrambles median -8.59 (37.5% higher); English median -8.05 (60% higher). log10 pattern mass: Z13 -7.66; scrambles -7.89 (36% at or above Z13); English -7.61 (52%). So the enumeration cannot tell Z13 from a random arrangement of its own symbols. The '22 good fits' figure comes from the repeat profile and says nothing about Z13's content. The report never says this.

'Roughly 20 to 60 equally good English readings' is wrong for generic text, and the conclusion is understated in one direction. In the truth-rank calibration, 20 of the 25 same-profile real phrases fall inside the 20k/<=4 space. Among those 20, the true phrase is the top fit in 6, in the top 10 in 17, has median rank 2 and a median LM-posterior share of 6.7%. So if Z13 were common-vocabulary English under simple substitution with no slip, its plaintext would probably be among the top ~10 fits (A DEFINITIVE AT, ON THE DEFEAT OF, IN THE DESERT IS, ON THE DEFECT OF, OF THESE NEWTON, ...). None of these is a credible answer to 'My name is', which disfavours that narrow hypothesis more than the report says. Caveat: the calibration truths are arbitrary sentence-initial cuts that often read like fragments too, so 'not a message' is a judgement, not a computation.

The 'good English' bar (median of sentence-initial fiction fragments, Web 1T word LM) systematically puts names, rare words, period vocabulary and Zodiac's misspellings below the bar. KATHLEEN JOHNS scores -10.01 and OF THESE MEN TOM -10.62, both below the -9.86 median. 5 of 25 English controls had words outside the 20k list. Given the 'My name is' framing, the 22-64 above-median counts are not the number of plausible readings. The name/pseudonym space is much larger (phase 1: 79,229 FIRST MIDDLE LAST fits). The claimed bound on 'how informative Z13 can be' therefore holds only for generic phrases.

The one-slip sentence 'The rise in the best score is expected when 13 wildcard positions are tried' was asserted, not computed. My null is tools/z13phrases_review_slipnull.js (simple substitution, 5k words, at most 4 words; no slip plus a wildcard at each of the 13 positions; results/z13phrases/review/slipnull_combined.json). Z13's best one-slip fit is OF THE DIRECTOR at position 6, -5.83, an improvement of 2.75 over its no-slip best. Of 36 scrambles of Z13's symbols, 2 reach -5.83 or better (AND DICTIONARY -5.64, THAT THEY DO NOT -5.72; empirical p = 0.081) and 3 of 30 match or beat the improvement (p = 0.129). Of 12 same-profile English controls, 1 reaches -5.83. The attacker's 'beats_null: no' is therefore right, and now backed by a computation. The pooled slip posterior also double-counts no-slip strings (111 of the top 2,000 slip06 fits put the circle's own letter at the wildcard) and uses a heuristic 1/26 factor; the effect is about 1%.

The full3_canonical_simple estimate ('about 27M +/- 6M strings') is selection-biased. It is extrapolated only from the 6 of 12 sampled tasks that finished within 120 s, so the slow, string-rich tasks are missing and the estimate is biased low. The code's note 'uniform random sample' does not hold here. Its estimate for fits at or above p50 is 0 +/- 0, although the run did find one (PATH ELEMENT PM). The only hard numbers are lower bounds: at least 1,780,143 strings and at least 1 fit at or above the median. Also, even complete, the full-vocabulary 3-word space covers only 49.9% of real 13-letter phrases (54.5% of those above the full-vocabulary median).

The real-phrase reference is 4,000 draws from only 17 held-out documents, with 27% duplicate draws (2,912 unique), and every phrase starts a sentence. Deduplicating shifts the 13-letter median from -9.861 to -9.904, p75 from -8.339 to -8.460, p90 from -7.191 to -7.345. The leave-one-document-out median ranges from -9.947 to -9.868. The canonical counts move to 24 simple and 69 homophonic at or above the median, and 1 and 4 at or above p75. The conclusions do not change.

Posterior and unscored-mass statements are stronger than the evidence. 'The unscored mass is under 3e-5' is a systematic 1-in-1000 sample estimate (2.6e-5). The rigorous bound in the same file is 8.1e-3. For the homophonic runs the unscored-mass bound is 189 times the scored mass and no sample estimate exists, so the homophonic shares (e.g. SOUTH THE HOUSE 17%) are not established.
Reporting inconsistency: the report says '13 theme hits in all runs', but summary.json has themeHitsAboveMedianCount = 16.

Requested or obvious analyses that are missing:
- Crosshair as a word boundary (task item 1). My check from the streams: 0 simple and 3 homophonic fits above the 12-letter median with a 3|9 split, so no change (results/z13phrases/review/crosshair_boundary.json).
- letters_literal pin subsets (the README allows subsets).
- Homophonic slips and homophonic null-letter runs.
- 6-word runs.
- circles_distinct at 60k/5.
- Full-vocabulary 3-word runs for the other variants.
- Misspellings that insert or delete a letter (e.g. ILL NEVE TELL IT). These lie outside the single-substitution wildcard.
- Transpositions other than reversal.
The attacker caveated most of these. None would yield a distinguished reading, because they only enlarge the fit space.

review.adjusted_conclusion:
The negative result stands, and the numbers reproduce exactly. No English word sequence is singled out by Z13 under any variant or substitution mode tested, and every highlighted candidate is unsupported. Two points should be added to the report.

(1) The enumeration statistics (fits above the real-phrase median, best fit score, total LM pattern mass) put Z13 in the middle of the distributions for random rearrangements of its own 13 symbols and for real same-profile English. So the dictionary search gives no evidence that Z13 is English at all. The '22 good fits' is a property of the repeat profile, not of Z13.

(2) The search is informative for generic common-vocabulary English. In a calibration on real phrases with Z13's profile, the true phrase had median rank 2 and was in the top 10 in 17 of 20 in-vocabulary cases. So the hypothesis 'Z13 is an ordinary common-word phrase, simple substitution, no slip' predicts that the plaintext is among the top ~10 fits. None of those (A DEFINITIVE AT, ON THE DEFEAT OF, IN THE DESERT IS, ...) is a plausible answer to 'My name is', which disfavours that narrow hypothesis. This relies on a subjective judgement of what counts as a message.

The 'about 20-60 equally good readings' bound does not cover the hypothesis the letter itself suggests, a name or pseudonym. Such readings fall below the LM median and number in the tens of thousands, so Z13 alone remains uninformative there. The one-slip reading OF THE DIRECTOR is within a computed scramble null (p ≈ 0.08 for its best-slip score). The full-vocabulary 3-word search covered about 5% of its tasks and its 27M-string estimate is biased low. Strength: none.
